messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Kofi's Burden

Kofi was sixty-two when his younger brother Kwame collapsed on a Lagos street during what should have been a routine business trip. The call came at 3 a.m. New York time—not from Kwame, but from a stranger at a hospital. Cardiac arrest, they said. Massive and sudden. By the time Kofi booked a flight, Kwame was gone. For three weeks after the funeral, Kofi moved through his Manhattan apartment like a man underwater, attending to the practical details—the will, the calls to relatives scattered across West Africa and the diaspora—but the actual moment of losing his brother remained fractured in his mind. He could recall the hospital corridor, the smell of antiseptic, the way his sister-in-law's voice had sounded when she told him Kwame was dead. But when he tried to deliberately reconstruct what happened in those final hours, when he attempted to piece together a coherent narrative of the day, the memory seemed to slip away from him. He knew Kwame had been meeting with investors. He knew it was hot. He knew the street was crowded. But the sequence, the precise details, the moment of collapse itself—these remained opaque, as though his mind had recorded only fragments and then locked them away.

This fragmentation tormented him. Kofi found himself obsessively replaying the events he could access, turning them over in his mind again and again, searching for the missing pieces as though repetition might unlock them. *Why had Kwame not called him the night before? Why had he chosen that particular street? Why had no one been there to help him in those first seconds?* The questions had no answers, but Kofi could not stop asking them. He began staying late at the office, sitting at his desk long after the markets closed, scrolling through old emails from Kwame, looking for clues, for some sign that he should have known, should have warned him, should have done something. His colleagues noticed the change—the distraction during client calls, the uncharacteristic errors in his portfolio management—but he said nothing. At home, he avoided the photographs on his shelves, the kitchen where Kwame had cooked jollof rice during his last visit two years earlier. He could not bear to see his brother's face, could not tolerate the sudden rush of grief that came when he encountered some unexpected reminder.

But avoidance only deepened the fragmentation. The more Kofi suppressed his thoughts about Kwame, the more those thoughts erupted unbidden—sudden, vivid pieces of memory that would ambush him without warning. A voice that sounded like his brother's in a restaurant would trigger a flash of the hospital corridor. A news story about cardiac events would bring the smell of antiseptic flooding back. These intrusions left him shaken, and in his fear of being overwhelmed by them, Kofi began to take risks he had never taken before. He drove recklessly on the FDR Drive, accelerating through yellow lights, as though speed might outrun the fragments. He began day-trading with increasingly aggressive positions, abandoning the conservative strategies that had built his reputation. He drank more—two glasses of whiskey became three, became a nightly ritual. Part of him knew these were dangerous, that they could destroy his career or his health, but another part of him felt that danger was appropriate, that he deserved it. What was the point of caution when death could come so suddenly, so senselessly, to someone forty years younger?

The recklessness fed the fragmentation. Each risky behavior brought with it a spike of adrenaline, a moment when Kofi felt intensely alive, but also a moment when his mind seemed to splinter further, when the fragments of memory appeared more violently and more frequently. And each time a fragment surfaced—a flash of Kwame's face, a sensation of helplessness—Kofi would suppress it again, push it down, try not to think about it. But the suppression only made the next intrusion more forceful. He was caught in a cycle he could not name but could feel tightening around him. The rumination continued, the questions unanswered. *Why him? Why not me instead?* The memories remained incomplete, inaccessible, yet somehow inescapable.

After eight months of this, Kofi's firm placed him on administrative leave following a series of poor trades. His ex-wife, with whom he had maintained cordial relations, called to say she was worried about him. He had missed a dinner with his daughter. He was, she said gently, not himself. It was this—not the symptoms themselves, which he had learned to live with, but the collapse of his professional life and the distance growing between him and his family—that finally brought him to a therapist's office. What Kofi feared most was not the fragments themselves, but that they would continue to fragment him, that he would lose everything Kwame's death had not already taken.
